When does an Arizona owner learn what the county thinks the house is worth?

Before March 1 each year, the county assessor must tell every owner of record what the property's full cash value is, along with its limited property value where one applies. That timing is set in A.R.S. 42-15101. For a seller, the notice is the first number to look at when you are deciding whether property tax is a problem on your sale.

The notice has to be in writing. The assessor can mail it or send it by common carrier, and can transmit it electronically if the taxpayer asks. The assessor also certifies to the board of supervisors and to the Department of Revenue the date on which all notices went out.

Two details often surprise owners:

  • The Department of Revenue director may push the mailing deadline back by up to thirty days when a flood, fire, other act of God or a declared emergency causes delays. If that happens it applies to every property the assessor values.
  • Within sixty days after the notices go out, the assessor may amend a notice if neighborhood or classification data produced a wrong opinion of value. Amended notices are sent only after the Department approves the new values.

After the mailing date you can still call the assessor and ask how a value was reached. The statute says the assessor may explain it but may not change the roll except through the review process the law provides.

What are the Arizona property tax due dates?

Arizona real property tax is paid in two halves: the first half is due October 1 and the second half is due the following March 1. The halves become delinquent at different times, which is where many sellers get caught.

InstallmentDueDelinquent after
First halfOctober 1November 1 at 5:00 p.m.
Second halfMarch 1May 1 at 5:00 p.m.
Total bill of $100 or lessOctober 1, all at onceDecember 31 at 5:00 p.m.

If a delinquency date lands on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, the cutoff moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. These rules come from A.R.S. 42-18052.

Notice the gap between the due date and the delinquent date. A bill is payable on October 1 but is not late until after November 1, so a house can close in October with the first half "due" and still unpaid without being delinquent. Your title company will say which amount it wants paid out of your proceeds.

What does the tax lien on an Arizona house mean for a sale?

A property tax in Arizona is a lien on the assessed property, and it attaches on January 1 of the tax year. That is stated in A.R.S. 42-17153. In plain terms, the house owes the year's tax before anyone has received a bill.

The same statute says the lien stays in place until one of three things happens:

  • The taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid.
  • Title has finally vested in a purchaser under a sale for taxes.
  • A certificate of removal and abatement has been issued.

The lien ranks ahead of other liens and encumbrances on the property, with two exceptions: liens held by the state and liens for taxes from other years. So a mortgage lender and a tax lien do not stand in line the way many owners expect. The tax sits at or near the front.

For a seller this has a practical side. If the buyer's title company finds unpaid tax, it will want that tax cleared at closing. The simplest way to avoid surprises is to ask the county treasurer for a statement of what is owed and what is coming before you sign anything.

What happens if property tax stays unpaid?

The county treasurer enforces unpaid delinquent tax by selling the tax lien and, later, foreclosing the right to redeem. A.R.S. 42-18101 gives the treasurer that job and says a small, insubstantial mistake in the process does not undo the assessment, the lien, the lien sale or the foreclosure of redemption rights.

That last point matters if you are hoping a technical slip will save you. The statute is written to protect the county's collection. The better path for an owner in trouble is to deal with the balance before the lien goes to sale, or to sell the house and have the balance paid from the proceeds.

The exact calendar for a lien sale, the interest rate and the redemption amount are set by other statutes and by each county treasurer.

What changes when the owner has died and a beneficiary deed is involved?

When a property passes by a beneficiary deed under A.R.S. 33-405, the assessor keeps mailing valuation notices to the late owner's last address until the beneficiary writes to the assessor. The beneficiary needs to send a certified copy of the last surviving owner's death certificate along with the new address. This rule appears in subsection B of A.R.S. 42-15101, and the law treats the old mailing as good delivery to the beneficiary.

The consequence is easy to miss. A notice can reach an empty house, and the sixty-day window to react to a valuation runs from the mailing, not from when someone actually opens the envelope. Heirs who are about to sell should do three things early:

  • Send the death certificate and a current address to the assessor.
  • Ask the treasurer whether either half of the current bill is delinquent.
  • Give the title company the parcel number so it can run the tax search.

Inherited houses with years of deferred repairs are common in our work, and tax status is often the first thing we check.

How does unpaid property tax affect a quick as-is sale?

A cash sale does not erase a tax lien, but it does move quickly enough that the tax can be settled at the closing table instead of growing for another season. If the house is behind on tax, the title company pays the county from your proceeds and gives you the net.

Here is how we usually walk an Arizona owner through it:

  1. Pull the parcel number from your last tax bill or the county records.
  2. Ask the treasurer for the current balance and which halves are open.
  3. Look at your valuation notice and decide whether the value is something you plan to challenge.
  4. Tell us the property's condition, any tenants and any liens you know about.
  5. Review the offer and the title company's payoff figures before you agree to anything.

We buy houses as-is, so the roof, the repairs and the clutter do not have to be solved first. The tax question is the one item that has to be answered with real numbers from the county.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Arizona valuation notice mailed?

Before March 1 each year, under A.R.S. 42-15101. The Department of Revenue director can extend the mailing by up to thirty days after a flood, fire, other act of God or a declared emergency. The notice states the full cash value and the limited property value if one applies.

When is Arizona property tax delinquent?

One-half is delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and the other half after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. If the whole bill is $100 or less, it is due October 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on December 31. A weekend or holiday cutoff moves to the next business day.

When does the property tax lien attach in Arizona?

On January 1 of the tax year. It stays until the tax, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a purchaser takes title in a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. It ranks ahead of most other liens.

Who sells the tax lien on an Arizona house?

The county treasurer. A.R.S. 42-18101 directs the treasurer to sell the tax liens on delinquent property and to foreclose the right to redeem. Ask the treasurer for the current payoff before you list or sell.

Do heirs get the valuation notice after the owner dies?

Not automatically. If the house passed by beneficiary deed, the assessor keeps mailing to the deceased owner until the beneficiary sends a certified death certificate and the new address. The old mailing counts as delivered to the beneficiary.

Who can claim the Arizona homestead exemption?

Any adult resident of Arizona can hold the exemption, whether married or single. The statute asks only that the person be at least eighteen years old and live in the state, and that the property be one the person actually lives in.

Three kinds of homes qualify. One is the person's interest in a single compact piece of land with a dwelling on it. Another is one condominium or cooperative unit. The third is a mobile home, park model, motor home, travel trailer, fifth wheel, houseboat, manufactured home or other shelter, plus the land under it.

A married couple or a single person gets one homestead only. The dollar figure measures the equity of the person or couple, not the home's price. If spouses lived in a home together and later divorce, the total protected for that residence cannot go above the statutory cap, no matter how the equity is split between them.

Do I have to file anything to get homestead protection?

No. The exemption exists by operation of law, so no written claim and no recording is needed to hold it. That surprises many owners, since some states require a filed declaration.

A filing matters in one situation. If you own more than one property that might fit, a creditor can send a demand letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, asking you to say which one is your homestead. You then have thirty days from receiving the letter to answer. You can answer by recording a homestead exemption with the county recorder where the property sits, or by sending the creditor a certified letter, return receipt requested.

If you ignore that letter, you can later assert the exemption only by recording a claim with the recorder. Anyone who receives a demand letter while trying to sell should treat the thirty days seriously and may want a lawyer to review the response.

What debts can still reach a homestead in Arizona?

The exemption blocks forced sale under most judgments and liens, but several claims get past it. The statute lists the exceptions, and a mortgage or deed of trust tops the list, because a lender you agreed to pay can still foreclose.

  • A consensual lien such as a mortgage or deed of trust, or a contract of conveyance.
  • A lien for labor or materials, claimed under the mechanics lien statute.
  • A lien for child support or spousal maintenance arrears, if the arrears were reduced to judgment, a lien exists under the family law statute, or the court ordered a specific security interest.
  • A recorded civil judgment or other involuntary lien, but only to the extent your equity is more than the exemption amount.

A sale that the exemption should have blocked is invalid and conveys no interest in the homestead. A court deciding a contempt case on unpaid support may also treat the exempt portion as a resource the payer could draw on.

How does a judgment creditor force a sale when equity is high?

A judgment creditor that is not a mortgage lender can ask for a judicial sale only when the debtor's interest exceeds the homestead amount plus all prior consensual liens. The officer running the sale cannot accept a bid unless it covers the debtor's homestead amount, the prior liens and the allowed costs of sale.

If a sufficient bid arrives, the proceeds are paid in a set order. The debtor receives the homestead amount first, then prior liens are paid, then costs, and whatever remains goes toward the judgment. If no sale happens, because the creditor drops the attempt or no one bids enough, the creditor cannot add sale costs or attorney fees to the judgment.

The practical lesson is that the exemption protects a set slice of equity and leaves the rest open to a creditor with a judgment.

What happens to my homestead protection after I sell?

The protection follows the cash. It attaches automatically to your interest in identifiable cash proceeds from a voluntary or forced sale and lasts eighteen months from the sale date, or until you set up a new homestead with the money, whichever comes first. It does not attach to cash taken out in a refinance.

Two practical points flow from this. First, keep sale proceeds identifiable, for example in a separate account, because the statute protects only identifiable cash proceeds. Second, the parties may rely on the valuation shown in the final closing disclosure when deciding how much equity existed on a sale or whether a refinance returned cash.

Only one homestead at a time may be held, so an owner who buys a replacement home before the eighteen months run out moves the protection to the new property.

When does Arizona treat a homestead as abandoned?

A homestead is abandoned by a recorded declaration, by deeding the property away or contracting to convey it, or by permanently moving out of the home or the state. Moving out temporarily does not end it, since a claimant may be away for up to two years without losing the exemption.

A declaration of abandonment or waiver must be signed and acknowledged by the claimant, and it takes effect only when recorded with the county recorder where the property is located. A recorded mortgage or deed of trust is not affected by the homestead claim at all.

One detail helps estate planners. Moving the home into a trust does not count as abandonment when the claimant keeps the power to run and revoke that trust.

EventEffect on the exemption
Recorded declaration of abandonmentEnds it from the recording date
Deed or contract to convey the propertyEnds it, except a transfer to a revocable trust you control
Moving out for up to two yearsDoes not end it
Permanent move from the home or stateEnds it
Sale of the homeMoves to identifiable proceeds for up to eighteen months

Is the homestead exemption the same as a property tax break?

No. The homestead exemption in title 33 protects equity from creditors, while property tax exemptions in title 42 reduce what the county bills, and they have different rules and different offices. Tax exemptions for widows, widowers, owners with disabilities and some veterans are filed with the county assessor by affidavit.

If you are bankrupt or may be, the statute adds a rule: the exemption amount is fixed as of the day the bankruptcy petition is filed. If the equity is at or below the cap on that date, the home is fully exempt, and later gains in value during the case stay exempt too.

The dollar cap also adjusts each January 1 for the consumer price index, rounded up to the nearest $100, so the figure you see quoted may be out of date. Check the current number with an attorney or the legislature's posted statute before relying on it.

How does this affect selling an Arizona house for cash?

An owner whose equity sits below the statutory cap has all of it protected from judgment creditors, so the homestead rules themselves rarely block a sale. The questions that deserve a closer look are liens that survive the exemption and what happens to the money afterward.

  • Order a title search early so mortgages, mechanics liens, support liens and recorded judgments are known before you agree on a price.
  • Ask the escrow officer how each lien will be paid from the proceeds.
  • If a creditor sent you a certified demand letter, note the thirty day response window.
  • Keep the proceeds in an identifiable account if you want the eighteen month protection.

A cash buyer can close without waiting for a lender, which helps when a lien payoff date is close. This page is general information, so have a lawyer review a specific situation before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Arizona homestead exemption automatic?

Yes. It exists by operation of law, so no recording or written claim is needed unless a creditor demands that you designate which of several properties is your homestead.

How long does homestead protection last on sale proceeds in Arizona?

It lasts eighteen months after the sale, or until you establish a new homestead with the proceeds, whichever is shorter. It does not cover cash from a refinance.

Can a mortgage lender foreclose on an Arizona homestead?

Yes. A mortgage or deed of trust is a consensual lien, and the exemption does not defeat it.

Can I leave my Arizona home for a while without losing the exemption?

Yes. A claimant may live away from the homestead for up to two years without abandoning it, but a permanent move from the home or the state does end the exemption.

Does a divorce change the homestead cap?

The cap does not double. For a home a couple shared before divorcing, the total exemption for that residence cannot exceed the statutory amount for either or both former spouses.

If Arizona has no estate tax, what could heirs owe on an inherited house?

The tax questions for heirs in Arizona are federal estate tax on very large estates and income tax on any gain after a sale. The state guide above covers Arizona's own position. This section covers the pieces that still reach an heir who is trying to sell a house after a death.

Most Arizona families who inherit a house face paperwork rather than a tax bill: who has authority to sign, whether a court must be involved, and how creditors are handled. Each of those has a statute behind it, and each can slow a sale if it is skipped.

When does federal estate tax apply to an estate that includes an Arizona house?

Federal estate tax applies only when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, exceeds the filing threshold for the year of death. The IRS estate tax page says most simple estates do not need to file a return.

The IRS lists these filing thresholds by year of death:

Year of deathFiling threshold
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

The IRS also notes that estates of decedents survived by a spouse may elect to pass along unused exemption on a timely filed estate tax return. The value used is fair market value at the date of death, not what the owner paid. That date-of-death value for the house is worth documenting even when no return is due.

Who can sell an inherited house in Arizona right after a death?

Only someone with legal authority can sign a deed, and in Arizona that is usually a court-appointed personal representative, a successor who has used a statutory affidavit, or a beneficiary named in a recorded beneficiary deed. Which path applies depends on how the owner held title.

Under A.R.S. 14-3715, a personal representative acting reasonably for the benefit of interested persons may sell, mortgage or lease estate real property for cash or credit, unless the will or a court order limits that power. The same statute lets the representative make repairs, insure the assets, and pay taxes and administration expenses from the estate.

If the personal representative has not yet been appointed, a buyer or an escrow officer will not close, because nobody can yet deliver good title.

Can heirs skip probate with an affidavit of succession?

Sometimes. A.R.S. 14-3971 lets successors file an affidavit for real property when the estate is small enough, and the statute sets specific conditions.

  • At least six months must have passed since the death, shown by a certified death certificate attached to the affidavit.
  • No application for a personal representative may be pending, and none may have been appointed, with real property in the estate valued at $300,000 or less after liens and encumbrances.
  • That value is taken from the full cash value on the assessment rolls for the year of death.
  • Funeral expenses, last illness expenses and all unsecured debts must be paid.
  • The signers must be entitled to the property as heirs or devisees, with no one else holding a right to it.
  • No federal estate tax may be due.

The affidavit is filed in the court of the county where the person lived, a certified copy is issued, and that copy is recorded with the county recorder where the house sits. The normal court filing fee applies unless it is waived.

A separate affidavit in the same statute covers personal property up to $200,000 after 30 days, which can help clear out a vehicle or accounts, but it does not replace the real property affidavit.

What if the owner recorded a beneficiary deed?

A recorded beneficiary deed can move title to the named person at the owner's death without probate. A.R.S. 33-405 says the deed must state that it is effective on the death of the owner and must be executed and recorded with the county recorder in the county where the property lies before the owner dies.

Points that come up for heirs:

  • The transfer is subject to mortgages, liens and other encumbrances the owner had at death.
  • An owner may revoke the deed any time before death by recording a revocation.
  • If more than one beneficiary deed is recorded, the last one recorded before death controls.
  • A beneficiary deed is not revoked by a later will.
  • If no named grantee survives the owner and no successor beneficiary is named, the deed is void.

The statute does not require the grantee beneficiary to sign or be told while the owner is alive, so some heirs learn of the deed only after the death. Check the county recorder's records early.

How long can heirs wait before opening an estate?

Arizona sets an outside limit of two years after death for opening most probate proceedings. A.R.S. 14-3108 says an informal probate or appointment, or a formal testacy or appointment proceeding, may not start more than two years after the death, with listed exceptions.

One exception allows a later proceeding if no court proceeding about the succession or administration has occurred within the two years. In that case the personal representative has no right to hold estate assets beyond what is needed to confirm title with the rightful successors, and claims other than expenses of administration cannot be presented.

Where there is no administration at all, A.R.S. 14-3901 says heirs and devisees take under the probated will or the laws of intestacy, subject to charges incident to administration, creditor claims and allowances to a surviving spouse and dependent children.

How do creditor claims affect the sale of an Arizona house from an estate?

Creditor claims can follow the house into the hands of heirs, so they are worth settling before or at closing. Under A.R.S. 14-3803, claims that arose before death are barred unless presented within the earlier of two years after death plus any notice period, or the time set by the statute for creditors who receive actual notice or publication.

The same statute says claims arising at or after death, including contract claims against the personal representative, are barred unless presented within four months after performance is due or after the claim arises, with the two-year rule applying for the later date on other claims. Enforcement of a mortgage or other lien on estate property is not affected by these limits, which is why a lender can still pursue the house itself.

What does the county recorder need at closing of an inherited house?

The recorder needs the deed and a completed affidavit of legal value. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires the seller and buyer, or their agents, to certify details such as names and addresses, the legal description, the date of sale, the total consideration, the type of financing and the assessor's parcel number.

The affidavit also asks whether a house will be owner-occupied or rented and whether the parties are related. The recorder must refuse to record without a complete affidavit unless the instrument bears a listed exemption.

An estate sale also needs whatever proves the seller's authority, such as letters from the court or the recorded affidavit of succession. The title company will tell you which documents it needs.

What are common problems for sellers of inherited Arizona houses?

The most common problems are missing authority, unpaid debts, and a house that has sat vacant. These are practical points, not tax rules, but each one affects how fast a sale can close.

  • No personal representative appointed, so no one can sign.
  • Heirs who live in different states and must all agree.
  • A mortgage or lien that survives the death and must be paid from the sale.
  • Back taxes or repairs that have piled up while the house sat empty.
  • Uncertainty about the value for date-of-death purposes.

A cash buyer can purchase a house as it stands, which removes repair work from the to-do list. The legal steps above still apply to the title.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona charge an estate tax or inheritance tax?

The guide above states that Arizona repealed its estate tax and does not impose an inheritance or gift tax. Federal estate tax is a separate matter and applies only above the IRS filing threshold, which is $15,000,000 for a death in 2026.

Can I sell an inherited Arizona house without probate?

Yes, if you hold title through a recorded beneficiary deed or you qualify to file an affidavit of succession for real property valued at $300,000 or less after liens, with at least six months passed since the death. Otherwise a court-appointed personal representative must sign.

How long do I have to open probate in Arizona?

The outside limit is generally two years after the death for most informal and formal proceedings, with exceptions listed in A.R.S. 14-3108.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, unless the will or a court order restricts it. A.R.S. 14-3715 lets a personal representative sell, mortgage or lease estate real property for cash or credit, acting reasonably for the interested persons.

What affidavit does the county recorder require for the sale?

An affidavit of legal value must be attached to the deed at recording. It states the parties, legal description, date of sale, total consideration and type of financing.

What are the steps of an Arizona eviction from filing to move-out?

An Arizona eviction moves from a written notice to a filed complaint, a short summons period, a hearing, a judgment, and then a writ of restitution that is carried out by law enforcement. For a rent case the whole path is measured in days or a few weeks, and each step has a rule behind it.

StepWhat the rules say
Notice period endsLandlord cannot file a nonpayment case until after the last day of the five-day notice
Complaint filedSummons issues the day the complaint is filed under A.R.S. 33-1377
Return dateNot more than six nor less than three days from the summons date
ServiceAt least two days before the return day
JudgmentPossession, late charges, costs and, at the landlord's option, unpaid rent
Writ of restitutionNot issued until five calendar days after judgment under A.R.S. 12-1178

How does service of the summons work?

The summons and complaint must be delivered to the tenant in one of two ways: personal service, or posting plus mailing. The Arizona courts' information sheet says the papers are generally served by a constable, sheriff or process server, either personally or by posting in an obvious place and mailing by certified mail.

Under A.R.S. 33-1377(B), the tenant is deemed to have received the summons three days after mailing when personal service was attempted, a copy was conspicuously posted on the main entrance within one day of issuance, and the summons was sent certified mail return receipt requested the same day.

The courts also say that a copy of the lease and related addenda must go with the complaint, and for a nonpayment case an accounting of charges and payments for the preceding six months must be attached.

What can a tenant do after being served?

The tenant may file a written answer or answer orally in open court on the record, and the court may order a written answer if it sets a trial date. The court's information sheet lists common defenses.

  • Rent was paid in full and on time, shown with proof of payment.
  • The landlord accepted rent with knowledge of the default without a signed writing setting the terms, which ties to A.R.S. 33-1371.
  • The tenant made repairs after proper notice and a licensed contractor did the work, with the cost, up to $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, subtracted from rent.
  • The tenant lives in subsidized housing with different rent rules.

The trial may be postponed for good cause supported by an affidavit for not more than three days in a justice court or five days in superior court.

Can a tenant stop the eviction by paying?

Often yes, but the price rises as the case moves forward. Under A.R.S. 33-1368(B), before the landlord files, the rental agreement is reinstated if the tenant tenders all past due rent and a reasonable late fee set out in a written rental agreement.

After the case is filed, reinstatement requires past due rent, late fees, attorney fees and court costs. After a judgment for the landlord, reinstatement is solely at the landlord's discretion.

For a house owner planning a sale, this matters: a tenant who pays in full before judgment keeps the lease, and the house stays tenant-occupied.

What does the judgment and writ of restitution do?

If the landlord wins, the court gives judgment for possession of the premises, late charges stated in the rental agreement, costs and, at the landlord's option, unpaid rent through the rental period, and grants a writ of restitution. This is set out in 33-1377(F).

The writ is held back for a short period. A.R.S. 12-1178 says no writ of restitution may issue until five calendar days after judgment, and filing a motion to set aside does not suspend or delay it unless a judge finds good cause.

A defendant who has been lawfully served with a writ and who remains in or returns to the dwelling without the owner's permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree. After a finding against the defendant, the court must give notice of that rule.

What happens to the tenant's belongings and the utilities?

The landlord may discontinue landlord-provided utilities the day after the writ is executed, and must then follow the personal property rules. A.R.S. 33-1370 requires the landlord to hold the tenant's personal property for fourteen calendar days after retaking possession and use reasonable care in moving and holding it.

After that period, if the tenant has made no reasonable effort to recover it, the landlord may donate or sell the property. Sale proceeds go toward the tenant's outstanding rent and covered costs, and any excess is mailed to the tenant. The landlord must keep records for twelve months after a sale.

The tenant may obtain clothing, tools of a trade, and identification or financial documents even before storage costs are paid.

What if the tenant leaves without telling the landlord?

The statute defines abandonment, and the landlord must follow a notice process before retaking the unit. Abandonment means the tenant is absent for at least seven days without notice, rent unpaid for ten days and no evidence of occupancy beyond belongings, or absent for at least five days with rent unpaid for five days and none of the tenant's property in the unit.

The landlord then sends a notice of abandonment by certified mail and posts it on the door for five days. After five days from posting and mailing, the landlord may retake the unit if no personal property remains. Money held as a security deposit is then forfeited and applied to rent and reasonable costs.

How are security deposits handled on a rented house that is sold?

The landlord's successor in interest is bound by the deposit rules. A.R.S. 33-1321 says the holder of the landlord's interest at the time the tenancy ends is bound by the section, so a buyer takes on the refund duty.

The deposit cannot exceed one and one-half month's rent, and within fourteen days after the tenancy ends and the tenant demands it, excluding weekends and holidays, the landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions. A landlord who fails to comply may owe the tenant twice the amount wrongfully withheld.

Can unauthorized occupants be removed differently from tenants?

Yes, in narrow cases. A.R.S. 12-1173 treats certain unauthorized occupants of a residence as forcible detainers if they refuse a reasonable request to leave and every one of several conditions is met.

  • The person asking is the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
  • The property is a residence or used for residential purposes, and the person is unlawfully there.
  • The occupant is not a current or former tenant, a family member, or someone with a prior agreement to live there.
  • No litigation is pending between the owner and the occupant.

For an action against an unauthorized person, a writ of restitution issues immediately after the court signs any judgment. A tenant at will or a month-to-month tenant whose tenancy has ended is a separate category under the same statute.

How does a pending eviction affect selling a rented Arizona house?

It adds risk and time but does not stop a sale by itself. A buyer who pays cash and buys as-is can take the house subject to the lease or wait for possession, and the choice depends on the court's progress.

  • A tenant who cures before judgment keeps the lease.
  • The writ cannot issue for five calendar days after judgment.
  • The landlord must show the house only on at least two days' notice at reasonable times.
  • Belongings left behind are held fourteen days before disposal.

If you want to avoid managing those steps, a direct sale to a cash buyer can include a move-out date agreed in writing.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an Arizona eviction take?

The court summons is returnable three to six days after it is issued, and a writ of restitution cannot issue until five calendar days after judgment. The total depends on notice, service, any postponement and the sheriff or constable schedule.

Can a tenant stay by paying after the case is filed?

Yes, if they pay all past due rent, late fees, attorney fees and court costs, and the landlord has not yet obtained judgment. After judgment, reinstatement is at the landlord's discretion.

How long must a landlord keep tenant belongings?

Fourteen calendar days after retaking possession under A.R.S. 33-1370, then the landlord may donate or sell them.

Is a tenant who stays after the writ breaking the law?

Yes. A tenant who is lawfully served with a writ of restitution and remains in or returns to the dwelling without permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree.

Does the new owner get the security deposit duty?

Yes. A.R.S. 33-1321 states that the holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules.

What makes an Arizona deed valid, including a quitclaim deed?

An Arizona deed has to be in writing, signed by the person giving up the property, delivered, and acknowledged before an authorized officer. A.R.S. 33-401 sets those rules for any conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or a term of more than one year. A quitclaim deed is held to the same basic standard as any other deed.

Signing is not enough on its own. Subsection B requires the grantor's signature and a proper acknowledgment, which is the notary step that lets the recorder accept the paper. If the acknowledgment has a flaw, the statute says a recorded deed is treated as properly acknowledged from the date it was recorded. That protects a deed after the fact, but you should not plan around it. Get the notary block right the first time, and have the notary complete every line before the signer leaves.

One extra rule applies to certain regulated grantees such as entities under titles 6, 10 or 29. Their full name, address and state of organization must appear in the deed, though the statute says a failure to include them does not make the deed invalid.

Does an Arizona quitclaim deed need an affidavit of property value?

Usually a deed needs one, but a quitclaim deed made for no money is exempt. A.R.S. 11-1133 says each deed that transfers title must have a joint affidavit of the buyer and seller attached at recording, and the county recorder must refuse any deed without a complete affidavit unless it carries a notation of an exemption.

The affidavit asks for plain facts about the sale:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers for buyer and seller.
  • The address for the tax statement, the legal description and the situs address.
  • The sale date, the total consideration and the down payment, and how the deal was financed.
  • Whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price was included.
  • The assessor's parcel number and the relationship between the parties.
  • Whether a house will be owner-occupied or rented.

An affidavit counts as complete when every item is answered or marked "not applicable." A blank line can leave the affidavit incomplete, so go through the form once more before you submit it.

Which Arizona quitclaim transfers are exempt from the affidavit and fee?

A quitclaim deed to quiet title or one executed for no monetary consideration is exempt, along with a short list of other transfers. The full list is in A.R.S. 11-1134. A few that come up for homeowners:

TransferStatute reference
Quitclaim to quiet title, or any quitclaim for no monetary consideration11-1134(A)(4)
Deed of gift11-1134(A)(7)
Conveyance made under a court order11-1134(A)(5)
Deed that confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed11-1134(B)(2)
Nominal-consideration residential transfer between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings11-1134(B)(3)
Transfer from a person to a trustee or from a trustee to a beneficiary, nominal consideration11-1134(B)(8)
Spouses to themselves to create community property with right of survivorship11-1134(B)(10)
Legal name change11-1134(B)(14)

The statute also requires that the exemption you claim be written on the face of the instrument at the time of recording. A deed that is exempt but does not say so can be refused like any other deed missing its affidavit.

What does a recorder look for on the quitclaim deed itself?

The recorder checks the form of the paper before anything else. A.R.S. 11-480 lists the conditions, and an instrument that fails one of them may be rejected when it is presented.

  • A caption that briefly states the nature of the document, such as "quitclaim deed."
  • An original that is legible enough to copy.
  • Original signatures, unless the law says otherwise.
  • For documents dated and executed on or after January 1, 1991, no wider than eight and one-half inches, no longer than fourteen inches, and type no smaller than ten point.

There is also a two-inch top margin on the first page for the recorder's stamp. The left three and one-half inches of that margin can show who asked for recording and where to return the document. If the first page does not comply, you attach a separate cover sheet that meets the requirement and shows the document's title. A half-inch margin applies on all sides, though failing it affects notice and is not a reason for rejection.

How much does the county recorder charge to record a quitclaim deed?

The standard county recorder fee in Arizona is $30 per instrument when no other fee is specified. A.R.S. 11-475 sets that figure, plus $15 per instrument for papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a political subdivision.

Certified copies cost $1 for each page or partial page, with $3 added for the recorder's certificate and seal. Check the recorder's own fee page for the county where the property sits before you send a check, since that office handles the filing.

Remember that the affidavit exemption in 11-1134 refers to "the affidavit and fee required by this article." The recorder's own fee in 11-475 is a different statute, so ask the recorder whether an exempt deed still pays the standard recording fee.

When does a quitclaim deed make sense if you plan to sell?

It makes sense when the goal is to fix or move title between people who already agree, such as removing a name after a divorce, adding a spouse, or moving a house into a family trust. It does not replace the sale paperwork when an outside buyer is paying for the house.

Think through these questions before you sign:

  • Who needs to be on title at closing? Ask the title company who must sign the sale deed.
  • Does a mortgage or tax balance remain? A deed between family members does not remove either one.
  • Is any money changing hands? Real consideration moves the transfer out of the no-money exemption and brings the affidavit back.
  • Will a title company insure the sale after the transfer? Ask before you record anything.

Is a quitclaim deed exempt from the Arizona affidavit of property value?

Yes, when it is a quitclaim to quiet title or is executed for no monetary consideration. A.R.S. 11-1134(A)(4) lists that exemption, and the exemption has to be written on the face of the deed at recording.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Arizona?

$30 per instrument is the standard county recorder fee under A.R.S. 11-475. Government-requested recordings are $15, and certified copies cost $1 per page plus $3 for the seal.

Does an Arizona deed need to be notarized?

Yes. A.R.S. 33-401 requires the grantor to sign and acknowledge the deed before an authorized officer. If the acknowledgment has a defect, a recorded deed is treated as properly acknowledged from the date of recording.

What size must an Arizona deed be?

No wider than 8.5 inches and no longer than 14 inches, with type no smaller than ten point, for documents executed on or after January 1, 1991. The first page needs a two-inch top margin for the recorder.

Can a quitclaim deed fix a mistake in an earlier deed?

A deed that confirms or corrects a previously recorded deed is exempt from the affidavit and fee under A.R.S. 11-1134(B)(2). Whether a quitclaim is the right tool for a given error is a question for a title company or attorney.

What is an Arizona beneficiary deed?

Arizona calls its transfer on death deed a beneficiary deed, and it passes real property to a named person when the owner dies. A.R.S. 33-405 says a deed that names a grantee beneficiary and expressly states it is effective on the owner's death transfers the interest at death, subject to every mortgage, lien and encumbrance the owner created or was subject to during life.

It names who receives the house at death. It does not change who owns the home today, and an owner who signs one remains free to sell, borrow against or live in the property.

How do you make an Arizona beneficiary deed valid?

It must be executed and recorded with the county recorder in the county where the house sits, before the owner dies. Subsection E of the statute makes recording before death a condition of validity, and a deed signed but left in a drawer does not work.

The statute also lays out what the deed can do:

  • Name several grantees, who can take as joint tenants with right of survivorship, tenants in common, community property, or another tenancy valid in Arizona.
  • Name a successor grantee beneficiary, with the condition that triggers the successor stated on the deed.
  • Convey to the trustee of a trust, even a revocable one.
  • Use the statutory form, which asks the owner to choose what happens if a beneficiary dies first: the gift becomes null and void, or becomes part of that beneficiary's estate.

If no named grantee survives the owner, the deed is void unless it says otherwise.

Can the owner change their mind or sell afterward?

Yes. The owner can revoke the deed at any time by recording a revocation before death, and no grantee has to sign or consent. Subsection I states that the signature, consent or notice to a grantee beneficiary is not required for any purpose during the owner's life.

Two more rules help a selling owner:

  • If more than one beneficiary deed is recorded for the same property, the last one recorded before death is the effective one (subsection G).
  • A later will does not revoke a recorded beneficiary deed (subsection J).

A sale made during life is one of the conveyances the beneficiary deed is subject to under subsection A. Whether a title company also wants a recorded revocation first is a question for that company.

Does a beneficiary deed clear mortgages and tax liens?

No. The transfer is subject to all conveyances, mortgages, deeds of trust, liens and other encumbrances. A beneficiary who receives the house receives the loan and any lien attached to it.

That has a practical effect on selling. A beneficiary who wants to sell must pay off a mortgage, unpaid property tax and other liens from the proceeds. If the house has a delinquent tax lien, the statutes covered on our Arizona tax lien and tax sale pages apply to the new owner just as they did to the old one.

What does it cost to record a beneficiary deed in Arizona?

The statutory recording fee is $30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475, and Cochise County lists the same flat fee on its recorder page.

The affidavit of property value and its fee are normally appended to deeds. Section 11-1134(B)(12) exempts a transfer made under a beneficiary deed with only nominal actual consideration, and section 11-1133 requires the exemption to be noted on the face of the instrument at recording. The recorder refuses a deed that has neither a complete affidavit nor an exemption notation.

How do joint owners and several beneficiaries change the picture?

Joint ownership changes who controls the outcome. When owners hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship or as community property with right of survivorship, a beneficiary deed signed by all surviving owners takes effect at the death of the last survivor (subsection D).

If fewer than all owners sign, the deed is valid only when the last surviving owner is one of the signers. If the last survivor did not sign, the transfer lapses and the deed is void. A surviving joint tenant or spouse keeps rights that prevail over the named grantee beneficiary.

With several beneficiaries, subsection B says that unless the deed provides otherwise, what each takes is that person's separate property and not community property. A house with three beneficiaries can therefore need three signatures at a sale, which affects how quickly a buyer can close.

What does the statutory form say?

The form in subsection K is short. It reads, in substance, that the owner conveys the described property to the grantee beneficiary effective on the owner's death, followed by the legal description and a choice about a beneficiary who dies first.

A separate revocation form appears in subsection L. It identifies the recorded deed by recording date and by docket, book, page or instrument number, and by county. The statute says a deed is sufficient if it complies with other applicable laws and substantially follows the form, so a recorder or title company will still look at the acknowledgment and the legal description.

What if the owner dies without a beneficiary deed?

Arizona offers affidavit routes for small estates, found in A.R.S. 14-3971. They help only when the numbers stay under the statutory limits.

For personal property, a successor can collect by affidavit 30 days after death when no personal representative is pending and the personal property, less liens, does not exceed $200,000.

For real property, a successor may file an affidavit of succession not sooner than six months after death. The real property in the estate, less liens, may not exceed $300,000, measured by the full cash value on the assessment rolls. The affidavit must state that funeral and last-illness expenses and all unsecured debts are paid, that the signers are entitled to the property by intestacy or a valid will, that no one else has a claim, and that no federal estate tax is due. A certified death certificate is attached, and the certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.

How does a beneficiary deed affect a cash sale after death?

The deed transfers the interest effective on the owner's death, so the beneficiary's title comes from the recorded deed. That title depends on the deed having been recorded before death and on no later revocation or later deed existing.

  • Is the recorded deed the last one on file for this property, and was it recorded before the date of death?
  • Did any named beneficiary die first, and what does the deed say about that case?
  • What mortgage balance and unpaid taxes sit on the house today?
  • Are there several beneficiaries who must all sign the sale?

A buyer paying cash for an as-is house can take on repairs, clean-out and a tenant, which is a common situation for an inherited property.

It is called a beneficiary deed under A.R.S. 33-405. It transfers real property to a named grantee beneficiary when the owner dies.

Does the beneficiary have to sign the deed?

No. The signature, consent or notice to the grantee beneficiary is not required during the owner's life.

When must the deed be recorded?

Before the owner's death, with the county recorder in the county where the property is located. Recording after death does not make a beneficiary deed valid.

Can I still sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?

Yes. The deed takes effect only at death, so a living owner can sell, and can revoke the deed by recording a revocation.

Does a will cancel a beneficiary deed?

No. A beneficiary deed that is executed, acknowledged and recorded as the statute requires is not revoked by a later will.

What if only some of the joint owners sign?

The deed is valid only if the last surviving owner is one of the signers. If the last survivor did not sign, the transfer lapses and the deed is void.

Does the beneficiary inherit the mortgage too?

Yes. The transfer is subject to mortgages, liens and encumbrances that existed when the owner died.

That timing matters when you sell. The lien sits on the parcel whether or not the current-year bill has gone out yet, so ask your title company early how the current year's tax will be handled at closing.

Where does the tax lien rank against a mortgage?

The tax lien ranks ahead of nearly everything else recorded against the house. The statute makes it prior and superior to all other liens and encumbrances, with two exceptions: liens held by the state, and liens for taxes of other years.

So a first mortgage, a second mortgage, a judgment lien and a contractor's lien all sit behind it. Three facts follow from the statute:

  • The lien is not satisfied until the taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, or until title finally vests in a purchaser under a sale for taxes, or until a certificate of removal and abatement is issued.
  • Selling the house does not erase it. The payoff has to come out of the sale proceeds.
  • Taxes from older years and from the current year can stack, and each year keeps its own lien.

What are the Arizona property tax due dates and delinquency dates?

Arizona splits the annual bill into two halves. Under A.R.S. 42-18052, the first half is due October 1 and the second half is due the following March 1.

A half becomes delinquent only after a later cutoff, and both cutoffs are at 5:00 p.m. If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or legal holiday, the cutoff moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

ItemDate or amount
First half dueOctober 1
First half delinquent afterNovember 1, 5:00 p.m.
Second half dueMarch 1 of the next year
Second half delinquent afterMay 1, 5:00 p.m.
Bills of $100 or lessAll due October 1, delinquent after December 31 at 5:00 p.m.
Interest rate on delinquent tax16 percent a year, simple

How much interest does a delinquent Arizona tax bill collect?

Delinquent taxes bear simple interest at 16 percent a year from the time of delinquency until they are paid. Section 42-18053 adds that a fraction of a month counts as a whole month.

As arithmetic, 16 percent simple works out to about 1.33 percent for each month. An unpaid $1,000 half-bill would add roughly $160 over a full year, and a part month is charged as a full one. The interest runs on the tax, not on a growing balance, which is what simple means.

The statute lists exceptions. Interest is not collected if the delinquency came from an error by the county assessor or treasurer. It is also not collected when the full year's tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year.

There is one more relief valve for owners who paid off a loan. With approval from the county board of supervisors, the treasurer may waive interest and other penalties for a delinquency that occurs within one year after a mortgage or deed of trust is satisfied or released. A taxpayer can receive that waiver only once per property.

What happens after taxes stay unpaid in Arizona?

The county treasurer sells the lien itself at an auction held in February, and the owner keeps title for now. Section 42-18101 directs the treasurer to secure unpaid delinquent taxes by selling the tax liens and, later, foreclosing the right to redeem.

The steps run in a fixed order:

  1. By December 31 each year, the treasurer prepares a list of real property with unpaid, delinquent taxes from prior years, and a notice that a tax lien on each parcel will be sold at public auction (A.R.S. 42-18106).
  2. The notice names the owner, the parcel number, the tax years that are delinquent, and the taxes, penalties, interest and charges.
  3. The treasurer posts the list at the office door for at least two weeks before the sale begins, and publishes it once in a county newspaper two to three weeks before the start date (A.R.S. 42-18109).
  4. The treasurer mails a copy of the notice to the owner of each listed parcel at the last known address (A.R.S. 42-18108).
  5. The sale is held in February (A.R.S. 42-18112).

A rule on timing also exists: a sale for unpaid tax generally cannot start later than five years after delinquency unless it was advertised within that period (A.R.S. 42-18105).

Who buys the lien, and what does the owner owe afterward?

Investors buy the lien, and the bidder who accepts the lowest interest rate wins. Section 42-18114 says the purchaser pays the whole amount of delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and charges, and offers the lowest rate on that amount, which may not exceed the statutory rate. Interest at the bid rate starts on the first day of the month after the purchase.

This is a lien sale and not a deed sale. The owner still holds title. What changes is the cost of getting clear. To redeem, a person pays the treasurer the sale amount with interest at the certificate rate, later taxes the purchaser paid with interest, and statutory fees the purchaser paid, excluding the processing fee (A.R.S. 42-18153).

What does a redemption certificate cost and where is it recorded?

The treasurer charges $10 for a full redemption when no partial payments were made. Under A.R.S. 42-18154, the treasurer issues a certificate of redemption once the right to redeem is established and the amount is paid, and the holder may record that certificate with the county recorder.

A recorded certificate is useful paper in a sale. It shows the buyer's title company that the lien sale was cleared. The statute also allows a $5 fee for the first and last partial payment, but partial payments apply to a county with a population above three million, so most rural owners will not use them.

How does a delinquent tax lien affect selling a house for cash?

A delinquent lien slows a retail sale but does not stop a sale to a cash buyer who prices it in. The unpaid tax, the interest and any lien-sale redemption amount are all deducted from what the seller receives at closing.

Practical points for an Arizona owner with a delinquent parcel:

  • Ask the county treasurer for the current payoff before you pick a closing date, since interest adds a whole month for any part of a month.
  • Check whether the lien was already sold at the February auction. If it was, the payoff is a redemption amount and not just back taxes.
  • Check older years. Other years' tax liens survive alongside the current one.
  • Keep any notice you received. The statute says an insubstantial failure to comply does not invalidate the lien or the sale, so a small defect will not make the debt disappear.

If the house also needs repairs or has a tenant, a buyer who purchases as-is can fold the tax payoff into the closing statement so you do not have to find cash first.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Arizona tax lien start?

It attaches on January 1 of the tax year, under A.R.S. 42-17153. The bill comes later, but the lien exists from that first day.

What is the interest rate on late property tax in Arizona?

The rate is 16 percent a year, simple, from the time of delinquency, and any part of a month counts as a full month. Interest is not collected if the full year's tax is paid by December 31 of the tax year, or if the delinquency came from a county error.

Does the tax lien come before my mortgage?

Yes. It is prior and superior to all other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for taxes of other years.

How can a delinquent Arizona owner get interest waived?

The treasurer may waive interest and penalties with board of supervisors approval, but only for a delinquency in the year after a mortgage or deed of trust was satisfied or released, and only once per property.

Can I sell my Arizona house if the county sold the tax lien?

Yes. You still hold title after a lien sale. The redemption amount is paid from the proceeds at closing, and the treasurer issues a certificate of redemption that can be recorded.

Who owns an Arizona house the moment its owner dies?

Ownership passes at death to whoever the will names, or to the heirs if there is no will, but it stays subject to the estate's debts and to administration. Arizona's probate code says a person's separate property and half of the community property go to the devisees or heirs, subject to the family allowances, exempt property and creditors' rights.

The surviving spouse's half of community property is a special case. It also stays open to administration until the time to present claims ends, and after that only to the extent needed to pay community debts.

In practice this means an heir cannot simply list the house the week after a funeral. Someone needs legal authority to sign, either a personal representative or a successor named in a recorded affidavit, so confirm which route applies before accepting an offer.

Is there a deadline to open an Arizona probate?

Yes, generally two years from the date of death. An informal probate, an informal appointment, or a formal testacy or appointment proceeding cannot be started after two years, subject to a short list of exceptions.

Exceptions include a will contest, which may begin within twelve months of the informal probate or two years from death, whichever is later. A late proceeding may also go forward if no court proceeding about the estate has occurred in the two years. In that case the personal representative has only the limited right to hold estate assets needed to confirm title with the rightful successors, and creditor claims other than administration expenses cannot be presented.

A missed deadline therefore does not always close the door, but it narrows what the representative can do, so heirs who inherited a house long ago should ask a probate attorney about timing.

Who can ask the court to open an informal probate?

The statute lists specific applicants, so not just anyone may file. The application goes to the registrar and must be verified.

  • The surviving spouse.
  • An adult child, a parent, a brother or a sister.
  • Any heir of the decedent.
  • A person nominated as personal representative in the will.
  • The Department of Veterans' Services, if the decedent was a veteran.
  • Any creditor, starting forty five days after death.
  • The public fiduciary, if no one else is qualified and willing.

The application must name the decedent, give the date of death and county of domicile, identify spouse, children, heirs and devisees, and state that the time limit has not expired. For a will, the original must be with the court or accompany the application, and the applicant must say the will appears validly signed and not revoked.

Who gets priority to serve as personal representative?

The order is set by statute, starting with the person the will names. If there is no will or the nominee will not serve, the statute works down a ranked list.

RankPerson with priority
1Person named in the will, including one named under a will's power to nominate
2Surviving spouse who is also a devisee
3Other devisees
4Surviving spouse
5Other heirs
6Department of Veterans' Services, for a veteran or a veteran's spouse or child
7A creditor, after forty five days
8Public fiduciary

An objection to an appointment can be raised only in a formal proceeding. Formal proceedings are also required when someone with higher priority has not renounced, when people share a priority and have not agreed, or when someone without priority seeks appointment. A person under the age of majority, a foreign corporation, or someone the court finds unsuitable cannot serve.

What does a personal representative have to do after appointment?

The representative has to inventory the estate and tell creditors about the death. Within ninety days of appointment, the representative prepares an inventory listing what the decedent owned, the value on the date of death, whether each item was community or separate property, and any encumbrance. It can be filed with the court or mailed to the heirs or devisees and to anyone who asks.

Creditors are warned in two ways. The representative publishes a notice once a week for three straight weeks in a county newspaper, and mails written notice to known creditors. A creditor generally has four months after first publication, or sixty days after receiving mailed notice if that is later, to present a claim.

Even without notice, the claim period is capped. Claims that arose before death are barred two years after death plus any time left in a notice period that was begun.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. The statute lets a personal representative acting reasonably for the interested persons acquire or dispose of an asset, including land in Arizona, for cash or on credit and at public or private sale. The representative may also sell, mortgage or lease estate real property, subject to anything the will or a court order restricts.

Supervised administration changes the process. In that setting, every sale of real property needs court confirmation, and the representative cannot make a distribution without a prior court order. A buyer or a title company will want to see letters showing the representative's authority and whether the estate is supervised.

After sale or when the house is distributed in kind, the representative signs a deed of distribution to the heir. Any deed of distribution recorded with a county recorder must list the name and address of each distributee.

When can heirs skip full probate for a smaller estate?

Arizona allows affidavits for small estates. If no personal representative has been appointed or is pending, successors can collect personal property by affidavit thirty days after death when it totals $200,000 or less after liens. For Arizona real property, a successor affidavit is allowed six months after death when the property, after liens, is no more than $300,000 in full cash value at death.

The real property affidavit has more conditions: debts and funeral expenses are paid, no one else claims the property, and no federal estate tax is due. A certified death certificate is attached, and the affidavit is filed with the superior court in the county of domicile. The registrar's certified copy is then recorded with the county recorder.

A buyer from a successor named in the recorded copy receives the same protection as a buyer from a distributee under a personal representative's deed of distribution.

How does a surviving spouse share when there is no will?

With no will, a surviving spouse takes the entire intestate estate when the decedent left no children or only children who are also the spouse's. If any child is not the surviving spouse's child, the spouse takes one half of the intestate separate property and nothing from the decedent's half of community property.

That split matters on a house. In a blended family, that can leave a house shared between a surviving spouse and children from another relationship, so ask who must sign the deed.

What should heirs gather before selling an inherited Arizona house?

Start with paperwork that proves who can sign. Having these ready lets you answer a buyer's questions quickly.

  • A certified death certificate.
  • The original will, if one exists, and the court's order or letters of appointment.
  • The deed or title report and payoff statements for any mortgage.
  • Property tax bills, since half is due October 1 and half March 1.
  • A list of heirs with current mailing addresses, for the deed of distribution.

This page is general information, not legal advice. For a contested will, an insolvent estate or a house with several heirs who disagree, consult a probate attorney.

Frequently asked questions

How long do you have to start probate in Arizona?

Generally two years from the date of death, with exceptions such as a will contest or a case where no court proceeding about the estate has occurred in those two years.

How long does a creditor have to file a claim against an Arizona estate?

Usually four months after the first newspaper notice, or sixty days after mailed notice if later. Claims are also barred two years after death, subject to the statute.

Does a personal representative need court approval to sell Arizona real estate?

Not in an unsupervised estate, where the representative may sell at public or private sale. In a supervised administration, every sale of real property needs court confirmation.

Can heirs sell an Arizona house without probate?

Possibly. A successor affidavit for real property is available six months after death when the property is worth $300,000 or less after liens and other conditions are met, and the certified copy is recorded with the county recorder.

When does the personal representative have to prepare an inventory?

Within ninety days after appointment. It lists the decedent's property, its date-of-death value, whether it was community or separate and any encumbrance.

How does Arizona tax the gain when you sell a house?

Arizona taxes a house sale gain through its individual income tax, and it lets you subtract part of a long-term gain. Under A.R.S. 43-1011, the state taxes the entire taxable income of residents and the Arizona-source income of nonresidents. A house is a capital asset, so a profit on the sale lands in that income unless a rule removes it.

Arizona has no separate capital gains tax line. The gain is a piece of your ordinary return, and the only gain-specific relief in the statute is a subtraction found in A.R.S. 43-1022, paragraph 22. That paragraph removes a share of net long-term capital gain that is included in federal adjusted gross income.

Two questions decide what you owe on a house: how much of the gain the federal home sale exclusion removes, and whether the rest qualifies for the Arizona subtraction.

What is the Arizona capital gains subtraction and who qualifies?

The subtraction is 25 percent of your net long-term capital gain for tax years beginning after December 31, 2014, but only for assets acquired after December 31, 2011. The statute phased it in: ten percent for 2012, twenty percent for 2013, then twenty-five percent from 2014 forward.

The phase-in table in paragraph 22 reads as follows.

Tax years beginningShare of net long-term gain subtracted
After Dec. 31, 2012 through Dec. 31, 201310 percent
After Dec. 31, 2013 through Dec. 31, 201420 percent
After Dec. 31, 201425 percent

A house bought before 2012 does not qualify, because the rule keys to the date the asset was acquired. If you cannot verify the acquisition date, the statute says the subtraction is not allowed, so keep the closing statement from your purchase.

Does the federal home sale exclusion help an Arizona seller?

Yes. The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on your main home, or up to $500,000 if you file jointly, and the excluded amount never reaches your federal adjusted gross income. Arizona's subtraction only applies to gain that is included in federal adjusted gross income, so the exclusion comes first and the state subtraction works on what is left.

The IRS explains the tests this way:

  • Ownership test: you owned the home at least 24 months out of the last 5 years before the sale.
  • Use test: you lived in it as your residence at least 24 months of that 5-year period. The 24 months of ownership and the 24 months of use do not have to fall in the same two years.
  • For a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • You generally cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home during the two years before this sale.

An Arizona rental house or a house you never lived in will usually fail the use test, which means the whole gain can be taxable.

Do you have to report a house sale if the gain is excluded?

Often yes. The IRS says that if you receive an information return such as Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable, and you must report it when you cannot exclude all of the gain.

Reporting runs through Form 8949 and Schedule D of Form 1040. For rules and worksheets the IRS points sellers to Publication 523, Selling Your Home.

If you sell in an installment arrangement, the IRS notes that the home sale exclusion remains available even when part of the price is paid in a later year.

How do federal long-term and short-term gain rules affect an Arizona house sale?

A house held more than one year produces a long-term gain, and a house held one year or less produces a short-term gain taxed as ordinary income. The IRS Topic 409 sets the line there, counting from the day after you acquired the asset through the day you sold it.

That line matters twice for an Arizona seller. Federally, long-term gain can qualify for lower rates. For Arizona, paragraph 22 reaches only long-term gain, so a house flipped inside a year cannot use the 25 percent subtraction.

For tax years beginning in 2025, the IRS lists these federal thresholds for the 0 percent rate on net capital gain:

Filing status0 percent rate up to taxable income of
Single or married filing separately$48,350
Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse$96,700
Head of household$64,750

The IRS says the rate on most net capital gain is no higher than 15 percent for most individuals, with a 20 percent rate above the 15 percent band. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent, which can matter if you claimed depreciation on a rental.

What happens if you inherited or were given the house?

For the Arizona subtraction, an heir or recipient of a gift is treated as having acquired the asset on the date the previous owner acquired it. The statute says a transferee who receives an asset by gift or at the death of the transferor is considered to have acquired it when the transferor did.

In practice that means an inherited Arizona house bought by a parent in 2005 would fail the post-2011 acquisition test, even if you inherited it last year. A house the parent bought in 2015 would pass it.

Your federal basis in an inherited or gifted house is not set by what you paid, and the IRS sends readers to Publication 551 for that rule. Because basis drives the size of the gain, get the date-of-death value documented, for example with an appraisal, before you list or sign a sale contract.

How do capital losses and the Arizona statute interact on a house?

A loss on your own home is not deductible. IRS Topic 409 states that losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home or car, are not tax deductible.

If the house was an investment and you sold at a gain, Arizona also lists a subtraction for the amount by which a capital loss carryover under A.R.S. 43-1029 exceeds the federal carryover, so a carryover from earlier years can matter. The federal limit on using net capital losses against other income is $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the rest carried forward.

What are the Arizona steps for recording a sale and how do they relate to tax?

Arizona county recorders require a sworn statement of sale details with each recorded deed. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, each deed and any sale contract must have an affidavit of legal value attached at recording, signed by buyer and seller or an agent.

The affidavit must disclose these facts, among others:

  • Buyer and seller names and mailing addresses
  • The legal description, situs address and assessor's parcel number
  • The date of sale and total consideration paid
  • Whether the financing was cash, a new third-party loan, seller financing, an assumption, or an exchange
  • Whether the house will be owner-occupied or rented

The county recorder must refuse to record a deed without a complete affidavit unless the document carries a listed exemption. The sale price on this form is the same figure you will use to compute your gain, so make sure it matches the settlement statement.

What should a seller keep to prove the gain?

Keep the purchase closing statement, receipts for improvements, and the final settlement statement from the sale. IRS Topic 703 says basis is generally what you paid, that improvements that add value increase it, and that allowable depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty losses reduce it.

A short checklist for an Arizona seller:

  • Closing statement from the purchase, which also proves the acquisition date for the 25 percent subtraction
  • Invoices for additions, a new roof, a new HVAC system, and similar capital work
  • The 1099-S or settlement statement showing gross proceeds
  • Records of days lived in the home, to prove the ownership and use tests
  • Any prior-year capital loss carryover worksheets

If the house needs work and you sell it as-is, only improvements you actually paid for can raise your basis.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona have its own capital gains tax rate?

No. Arizona taxes a house sale gain as part of your individual income, and the statute offers a subtraction of 25 percent of net long-term capital gain from assets acquired after December 31, 2011. For the current income tax rate that applies to your return, ask the Arizona Department of Revenue or a tax professional.

Can I use the 25 percent subtraction on a house I bought in 2008?

No. The subtraction in A.R.S. 43-1022 applies only to gain from an asset acquired after December 31, 2011, so a 2008 purchase does not qualify.

What if I cannot prove when my parent bought the house I inherited?

The subtraction is denied. The statute says that if the acquisition date cannot be verified, no subtraction is allowed, and for an inherited house the date that counts is the one on which the person who died acquired it.

Do I owe tax if I lived in the house for two years?

You may owe nothing federally on gain up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests. Any gain above those limits is still reported and may be taxed, and you must report the sale if you receive a 1099-S.

Is a loss on my house deductible in Arizona?

No. The IRS says losses from the sale of personal-use property such as a home are not deductible.

How does an Arizona tax sale work?

Arizona holds a tax lien sale first, and a deed only follows if the lien is never redeemed. The county treasurer sells the lien on delinquent real property at public auction in February, and the buyer receives a certificate of purchase and not the house.

The owner keeps title, the right to live there and the right to sell. The sale simply puts an investor in line to collect interest, and later to sue for the property if nobody redeems. That two-stage design gives an owner more time than many people expect, but the clock does run.

What stages does an Arizona tax sale go through?

There are four stages from first delinquency to a possible deed. Each stage has its own statute, and each is a point where you can step in.

StageWhat happensStatute
DelinquencyTaxes unpaid after the November 1 or May 1 cutoff at 5:00 p.m.42-18052
Lien saleTreasurer sells the lien at auction in February42-18112
Redemption windowOwner or others may redeem any time within three years, and after that until a treasurer's deed is delivered42-18152
Foreclosure suitLien holder sues in superior court to foreclose the right to redeem42-18201

The first three rows can run for years before the fourth begins, which is why a delinquent parcel can sit quietly while interest builds.

Who can bid, and how is the winner picked?

The winning bidder pays the whole delinquent amount and offers the lowest interest rate. Section 42-18114 says the rate may not exceed the cap computed under section 42-18053, and interest at the bid rate runs from the first day of the month after the purchase.

Bidding down the rate is the opposite of an ordinary auction, because a lower rate beats a higher one. The treasurer continues the sale from day to day, excluding Sundays and holidays, until each parcel has been offered and no more bids come in (A.R.S. 42-18112).
