How long does an owner have to redeem after the lien is sold?

The owner can redeem within three years of the sale date, and after that until the treasurer delivers a deed. Section 42-18152 states both periods.

Redemption costs three things, set out in 42-18153:

  • The amount the lien sold for, with interest at the rate on the certificate of purchase.
  • Taxes that accrued after the sale and were paid by the purchaser, with interest at the same rate.
  • Statutory fees the purchaser paid in connection with the certificate, excluding the processing fee.

The treasurer then issues a certificate of redemption, and the holder may record it with the county recorder.

When can the lien buyer sue to take the house?

No earlier than three years after the sale, and no later than ten years after the last day of the month in which the lien was acquired. Section 42-18201 lets the purchaser, or the state if it holds the lien, file an action to foreclose the right to redeem.

The suit goes in the superior court of the county where the property sits and must name the county treasurer as a party. If a law or court order prohibits filing, the deadline extends by twelve months after that prohibition ends.

This is the stage where an owner stops being able to wait. Papers served in a foreclosure action should be read the day they arrive, and an owner can still redeem by paying the redemption amount until a judgment ends the right.

What is an excess proceeds sale in Arizona?

It is a court-ordered sale of the house when the property is worth enough above the lien amounts that the owner's equity deserves protection. Under A.R.S. 42-18204, the court finds a sale reasonable if the likely sale price is more than $2,500 above the total owed to the lien holder.

Either side can ask for the finding. The lien holder reports its costs, the lien amount with 16 percent interest from the date of sale, and fees. The owner provides a reasonable estimate of market value. If the request is granted, the court orders a sale and sets an opening bid, and the owner's interest in the excess proceeds survives.

If the court finds no reasonable excess sale, it enters judgment foreclosing the right to redeem and directs the treasurer to deliver a deed to the party who won. After that judgment, the former owner has no further right, title or interest in the property, subject to appeal. Easements and certain assessment liens are not extinguished.

What notice will an Arizona owner receive before the sale?

The treasurer must mail a copy of the notice of proposed sale to the owner at the last known address (A.R.S. 42-18108). That makes an outdated mailing address a real risk for inherited homes and rentals.

The notice also appears in two public places. The list is posted at the treasurer's office door for at least two weeks before the sale starts, and published once in a county newspaper two to three weeks before the start date. If the treasurer misses a minor step, the statute says an insubstantial failure to comply does not invalidate the sale.

How long can the whole process take?

The statutes set a minimum and a maximum, and the gap between them is wide. Nothing in the process can produce a foreclosure suit sooner than three years after the lien sale.

Point in timeRule
February of the sale yearLien auction held (42-18112)
Up to five years after delinquencyWindow to commence a sale for unpaid tax, unless advertised within that period (42-18105)
Three years after the saleEarliest date to file a foreclosure action (42-18201)
Ten years after the month the lien was acquiredLatest date to file, with a twelve month extension if a law or order blocks filing (42-18201)

An owner reading these dates should treat the three year mark as a real deadline for planning, even though redemption stays possible after it.

Can I sell my Arizona house before the tax sale or after it?

Yes, at either point, because the owner keeps title until a deed is delivered. Selling before the February auction means the delinquent taxes and interest are paid from the proceeds. Selling after the lien sale means the redemption amount is paid instead.

Points to settle before closing:

  • Get the treasurer's payoff figure in writing and check for older tax years, since liens for other years survive.
  • Ask whether a certificate of purchase exists and who holds it.
  • Confirm that no foreclosure action is already pending in superior court.
  • Expect the deed to carry an exemption note or an affidavit of property value, and expect a recording fee of $30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475.

A buyer who pays cash and takes the house as-is can often close faster than a financed buyer, since there is no lender appraisal to wait for.

Frequently asked questions

Does Arizona sell the house at a tax sale?

Not at the first stage. The county sells the tax lien, and the owner keeps the house. A deed follows only if the lien holder wins a foreclosure of the right to redeem.

How long do I have to redeem an Arizona tax lien?

Three years after the lien sale, and after that until the treasurer delivers a deed to the certificate holder. Redemption is paid to the county treasurer.

Can an investor sue right away after buying the lien?

No. A foreclosure action can start no earlier than three years after the sale, and it must be filed within ten years after the month the lien was acquired.

What happens if my house is worth much more than the tax debt?

Either side can ask the court for an excess proceeds sale. The court treats it as reasonable if the likely price is more than $2,500 above what the lien holder is owed, and the owner's interest in the excess survives.

What interest does the lien holder charge?

The lien accrues interest at the rate bid at auction, which cannot exceed the 16 percent statutory cap. In a foreclosure action, the lien holder's amounts are figured at 16 percent a year from the date of sale.

Where do I record a certificate of redemption?

At the county recorder's office in the county where the property is located. Recording it is optional but helps a title company see the lien was cleared.

What do you need in hand before you try to record a deed in Arizona?

You need the signed and notarized deed, a completed affidavit of property value or a stated exemption, and the recording fee. Those three items cover what most recorders turn away at the counter. The deed rules come from A.R.S. 33-401 and the affidavit rules from A.R.S. 11-1133, and the county recorder applies both when a document is presented.

A short pre-flight list helps:

  • The original deed with original ink signatures. Photocopies do not meet the statute for original documents.
  • A notary acknowledgment on the deed, completed by an officer authorized under Arizona law.
  • A caption near the top that names the document, for example "warranty deed" or "special warranty deed."
  • The assessor's parcel number and the full legal description.
  • The address where the tax bill should go.
  • The affidavit of property value, signed by both parties or their agents, or a clear exemption notation.
  • A check or payment method accepted by the recorder in that county.

Where is a deed recorded in Arizona, and who does it?

A deed is recorded with the county recorder, and in a typical sale the title or escrow company delivers it for you after funds are in. The statute that governs recording fees, A.R.S. 11-475, is written around the county recorder's office, and the affidavit statute refers to the same officer.

For a cash sale, closing and recording happen in a set order. The buyer's funds are deposited, the title company confirms the payoff figures, the deed is signed, and then the document goes to the recorder. Sellers sometimes assume the sale is final when they sign, but the public record is updated only after the recorder accepts the deed.

The county recorder where the property sits is the office that matters, because the statute places recording at that office and nowhere else. If you own a house in one county and live in another, you still deal with the first county's recorder.

How much does recording cost, and what do certified copies cost?

The default Arizona recorder fee is $30 per instrument, and certified copies cost $1 per page plus $3 for the recorder's seal. A.R.S. 11-475 sets out the schedule:

ServiceFee
Recording papers with no other fee specified$30 per instrument
Papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a political subdivision$15 per instrument
Certified copy of a record$1 per page or partial page
Recorder's certificate and seal on a copy$3 added
Certificate under section 47-9523$10 per name, plus $1 per financing statement

Two more details are useful. State agencies that ask for copies for official purposes pay half the copy fee. Recorders also may not charge a county office that needs a document recorded when the fee would come from public money.

What formatting rules can get an Arizona deed rejected?

An instrument can be rejected at presentation if it lacks a caption, is not an original, is hard to read, lacks original signatures or exceeds the size limits. Those grounds are listed in A.R.S. 11-480, and the statute treats them as the complete list of reasons to refuse at the counter.

The numbers to remember are short:

  • Width of 8.5 inches or less and length of 14 inches or less for documents executed on or after January 1, 1991.
  • Type no smaller than ten point.
  • A half-inch margin around the page edges. Text inside it may not count as notice unless the recorder's copy reproduces it, but this alone does not allow rejection.
  • A top margin of at least two inches on page one, kept clear for the recording stamp.

If a document changes an earlier recorded document, it must state the earlier recording date and the docket and page. Once a document is accepted, the statute says it cannot later be attacked for failing these form rules.

What is the affidavit of property value and when can you skip it?

The affidavit is a joint form signed by seller and buyer that lays out price, financing and parties, and the recorder must refuse a deed that lacks one unless an exemption is noted. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires it for each deed that transfers title and each contract for sale of real property.

It also asks whether personal property was part of the price, how the sale was financed (cash, new third-party loan, seller loan, assumed loan or exchange) and whether the buyer plans to live in the house or rent it. Foreclosed trustee's deed beneficiaries who receive extra insurance money have a separate declaration to file within four months.

The exemptions are listed in A.R.S. 11-1134. They include deeds of gift, court-ordered conveyances, sales for delinquent taxes, partitions, transfers into or out of a joint tenancy, and transfers caused by a legal name change. Whatever exemption applies must be marked on the face of the deed, naming the specific one claimed. A general note that the transfer is exempt does not satisfy the statute.

Does a flaw in the notary block ruin a recorded Arizona deed?

Not after recording. Under A.R.S. 33-401(D), a recorded deed with a defect, omission or informality in the acknowledgment, or a lapse in how it was taken, is treated as duly acknowledged from its recording date.

This is a safety net for the past, not a plan for the future. Ask your title company whether it wants a corrected deed before the sale closes. If you spot an error on a deed before it is recorded, fix it before it is recorded.

How does recording tie into selling a house fast in Arizona?

Recording is the last step of the sale, so any problem with the deed holds up the day the buyer's name appears on the record. That is why the title company reviews the deed form before closing and why we ask sellers to send us the vesting deed early.

When a seller wants to sell quickly, these items usually decide how smoothly the recording goes:

  1. The name on the deed matches the name on the seller's ID.
  2. Any owner who has died has been dealt with through the proper estate or deed steps.
  3. Liens, tax balances and loans have payoff figures.
  4. The affidavit of property value is filled in or an exemption is marked.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Arizona?

With the county recorder in the county where the property sits. In a sale, the title or escrow company normally submits the deed after the buyer's funds are in.

What is the Arizona deed recording fee?

$30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475 when no other fee is stated. Documents recorded at the request of a government body are $15 per instrument.

What can cause an Arizona recorder to reject a deed?

A missing caption, a non-original or illegible document, missing original signatures, or a document wider than 8.5 inches, longer than 14 inches or set in type smaller than ten point. A missing affidavit without an exemption notation is also a reason to refuse.

Do I need a notary to record a deed in Arizona?

Yes. A.R.S. 33-401 requires the grantor's signature and an acknowledgment before an authorized officer. A recorded deed with an acknowledgment defect is treated as properly acknowledged from the recording date.

How much is a certified copy of a recorded deed?

$1 for each page or partial page, plus $3 for the recorder's certificate and seal, according to A.R.S. 11-475.
